# Introduction

This vignette is written as teaching material. It assumes that you can read R
code and that you have met a table of variant calls before, but it assumes
nothing about population genetics or about Bioconductor containers. Every term
is defined where it first appears, and the Glossary near the end collects the
definitions in one place.

## What an iSNV is

When a pathogen replicates inside one host, its genome is copied imperfectly.
After a few days the host carries not one genome but a population of closely
related genomes. If a sample from that host is sequenced deeply, most positions
give reads that all agree, while at a few positions some reads carry one base
and some carry another. Such a position is an **intra-host single nucleotide
variant**, abbreviated **iSNV**: a single-base difference that segregates
*within* one host rather than between hosts.

Two numbers describe an iSNV. The **allele frequency** is the proportion of
reads carrying the non-reference base, so a frequency of 0.08 means that 8% of
the reads at that position disagree with the reference. The **read depth** is
how many reads covered the position at all. The two are inseparable: 8% of 2,000
reads is 160 independent observations, while 8% of 25 reads is two reads and
could easily be sequencing error. Within-host variation lives at low
frequencies, which is exactly where sequencing and amplification artefacts also
live, so an analysis that does not carry depth alongside frequency cannot tell
the two apart (McCrone and Lauring 2016).

## What this package is for

Researchers studying within-host pathogen evolution work with tools that do not
fit together. Variant callers such as iVar, LoFreq and Freebayes write their
output in different formats. Quality control is usually done by ad hoc scripts,
which delete the calls that fail a threshold and so prevent any re-analysis
under another threshold. Donor and recipient samples, technical replicates and
sampling days are tracked in spreadsheets beside the data rather than in the
data.

`WithinHostExperiment` closes that gap. It provides:

-   a container built on `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("SummarizedExperiment")`, which
    keeps the call matrix, the genomic coordinates, the sample metadata and the
    quality-control history in one object;
-   replicate-aware quality control that flags rather than deletes, so that
    every call survives for re-analysis;
-   within-host diversity, site frequency spectra, neutrality statistics and a
    within-host selection ratio;
-   standardised export for downstream transmission bottleneck estimation.

## What this package does not do

The package works one site at a time. It does not reconstruct haplotypes, does
not separate a co-infection from genuine within-host diversity, and does not fit
drift-aware selection models. The section on scope and limitations sets out each
of these, with pointers to tools that do them.

## Relationship to existing tools

-   iVar, LoFreq and Freebayes (variant calling): upstream; we read their
    output.
-   `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("deepSNV")` (low-frequency variant detection):
    upstream and complementary.
-   ViralBottleneck (bottleneck estimation): downstream; we export to it.
-   `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("QSutils")` (quasispecies diversity): parallel, at
    haplotype granularity.

## Why Bioconductor

The package belongs in Bioconductor rather than on CRAN for four reasons. It
operates on high-throughput sequencing data, which is Bioconductor's own domain.
It extends `RangedSummarizedExperiment` and interoperates with `GRanges`,
`VRanges` and the `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("VariantAnnotation")` ecosystem rather
than inventing containers. It is complementary to existing packages, sitting
between upstream callers and downstream bottleneck estimators. And its
flag-rather-than-delete philosophy, with a full audit log on the object, matches
Bioconductor's emphasis on reproducible workflows.

## A warning about the example numbers

Every data file used below is synthetic, with one exception: the worked example
on real data uses two small per-sample tables from Bendall et al. (2023), which
are real but tiny. The synthetic files were written to exercise the code paths,
not to resemble an infection. Their frequencies, diversity indices, bottleneck
estimates and selection ratios therefore show the *form* of each output and
carry no biological meaning whatever. We say so again at each result, because a
number printed by a vignette is easily mistaken for a finding.

# Installation

The package is distributed through Bioconductor, which keeps every package in a
release aligned to one version of R, so that a workflow built today can be
rebuilt later. The installer is `BiocManager`, a small CRAN package that
resolves the right Bioconductor release for the R you are running; installing a
Bioconductor package with `install.packages()` instead will usually fail or
fetch a mismatched version.

The chunk below installs `BiocManager` if it is missing, then installs this
package and its dependencies. It is not evaluated when the vignette is built,
since the package is already installed at that point.

```{r install, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("WithinHostExperiment")
```

`BiocManager::install()` prints the packages it will fetch and then the usual
download and compilation messages. If it reports that your Bioconductor version
is out of date, run `BiocManager::install(version = ...)` for the release that
matches your R, or update R first. The README describes how to obtain the
development version, which is useful only if you need a change that has not yet
reached a release.

Once installed, the package is attached like any other. Attaching it also makes
the S4 generics and the `show` methods used throughout this vignette available.

```{r library, message=FALSE}
library(WithinHostExperiment)
```

A silent return means success. The examples below also use `GenomicRanges` for
genomic intervals, so we attach that too; everything else is called with the
`::` operator so that you can see which package each function comes from.

```{r library-gr, message=FALSE}
library(GenomicRanges)
```

Again nothing is printed. We are now ready to look at the container itself.

# The WithinHostExperiment object

A `WithinHostExperiment` extends `RangedSummarizedExperiment`, the standard
Bioconductor container for a rectangle of measurements. Three ideas carry over.
The **rows** are features, here variant sites, and their coordinates live in
`rowRanges()` as a `GRanges`. The **columns** are samples, and their metadata
lives in `colData()` as a table with one row per sample. The **assays** are
matrices of the same shape, rows by columns, one matrix per measured quantity,
reached with `assay(x, "name")`. Because every matrix shares one set of rows and
one set of columns, subsetting the object subsets the coordinates, the sample
table and every matrix together, and they cannot fall out of step.

The package ships a small synthetic example so that the structure can be
inspected without importing anything. Printing an object calls its `show`
method, which gives a summary rather than the contents.

```{r object-show}
data(example_whe)
example_whe
```

The first line gives the shape: 28 variant sites by 3 samples. The second lists
the five assays. The `show` method then adds two lines of its own. `qcLog`
reports how many quality-control steps have been recorded in the first slot this
class adds, zero so far because no filter has been run. `transmission pairs` is
not a slot: it is computed from the sample table by `transmissionPairs()` each
time the object is printed, and reports one donor-and-recipient pair here. The
second added slot, `qcFilters`, is not printed in the summary and has to be
asked for, as shown two sections below. Nothing in the summary tells you whether
the data are any good; that is what the rest of the vignette is for.

## The standard assays

Each assay answers one question about every site in every sample, and they are
used together rather than separately. `altCount` and `refCount` are the numbers
of reads carrying the alternative and the reference allele; `totalDepth` is the
read depth; `altFreq` is the allele frequency; and `qcPass` is a logical matrix
recording whether that call passed quality control. Only `altFreq` is strictly
required, and `qcPass` is created as all-`TRUE` when it is not supplied.

```{r object-assays}
SummarizedExperiment::assayNames(example_whe)
head(SummarizedExperiment::assay(example_whe, "altFreq"), 4)
```

The names come back in storage order, and the first four rows of `altFreq` show
one column per sample. The `NA` entries matter: they are not zero frequencies
but sites where that sample has no call at all, because a variant caller lists
only the positions it reported. A zero would assert that the sample was examined
there and found nothing; `NA` asserts nothing. Every function in the package
distinguishes the two, and so should any code you write against the object.

## The row ranges

`rowRanges()` holds one genomic interval per site, with the reference and
alternative alleles as metadata columns. Keeping the coordinates in a `GRanges`
is what lets the annotation functions overlap the sites with genes without any
coordinate arithmetic on your part.

```{r object-rowranges}
head(SummarizedExperiment::rowRanges(example_whe), 3)
GenomeInfoDb::seqlengths(example_whe)
```

Each row shows the sequence name, the position as a one-base range, the strand,
which is `*` because a variant site has no strand, and the `ref` and `alt`
alleles. The `seqlengths()` call then reports the recorded length of each
sequence, here 1,000 bases for the synthetic segment. That length is a property
of the reference the calls were made against, and the per-site diversity indices
read it from here rather than taking it as an argument, so it cannot be mistyped
into one function and not another.

## The sample table

`colData()` carries one row per sample. One column is required, `sample_id`, and
five more are recognised where they are present: `host_id` for the host a sample
came from, `replicate_group` and `replicate_id` for technical replicates, and
`role` (one of `donor`, `recipient` or `independent`) with `pair_id` for
transmission pairs. Any other column you add is carried along untouched.

```{r object-coldata}
SummarizedExperiment::colData(example_whe)
```

The three samples here are a donor, a recipient and an unrelated host, with the
first two sharing `pair_id` of `pair_1`; the extra `ct_value` column is study
metadata that the package ignores. These columns are how the analysis functions
find their groups: the transmission functions read `role` and `pair_id`, the
replicate filter reads `replicate_group`, and the longitudinal functions read
`host_id` and `timepoint`. A missing column is the usual reason such a function
reports that it found no groups.

## The first added slot: qcLog

Quality control that deletes rows destroys the evidence for its own decisions.
This package flags instead, and records each decision in a slot called `qcLog`:
a `DataFrame` with six columns, `step` (which filter ran), `parameter` and
`value` (the threshold it used), `n_flagged` (how many site-by-sample cells that
step newly failed), `n_passed` (how many still pass afterwards) and `timestamp`.
Read in order, the rows are a transcript of what was done to the object.

A `RangedSummarizedExperiment` cannot hold this. Its `metadata()` is a plain
list: it will accept a log under any name, with any columns, or none, and
nothing checks it. A reader of the object could not then rely on a log being
present, on its columns, or on its meaning, and two scripts would invent two
incompatible conventions. Making it a slot with a validity method turns the log
into part of the contract of the class. The accessor is `qcLog(x)`, and the
replacement form `qcLog(x) <- value` lets code outside this package append its
own steps.

```{r object-qclog}
qcLog(example_whe)
```

A `DataFrame` with 0 rows and 6 columns is an untouched object: the six columns
exist, so the structure is there to be read, but no filter has run. This is the
state after import, and any analysis that reports diversity from an object in
this state is reporting unfiltered calls.

The replacement form matters for interoperability, so it is worth seeing. Here
we append one row recording a manual review step, which no function in this
package performs, and print the log without its timestamp column so that the
output does not change between builds.

```{r object-qclog-replace}
example_qc <- flagISNV(example_whe, ISNVFilter(minDepth = 1000L))
reviewed <- example_qc
extra <- S4Vectors::DataFrame(
    step = "manual_review", parameter = "reviewer",
    value = "two sites re-checked by eye", n_flagged = 0L,
    n_passed = sum(SummarizedExperiment::assay(example_qc, "qcPass")),
    timestamp = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S"))
qcLog(reviewed) <- rbind(qcLog(example_qc), extra)
qcLog(reviewed)[, c("step", "parameter", "value", "n_flagged", "n_passed")]
```

The first four rows were written by `flagISNV()`, one per threshold it applied,
and the fifth is ours. `n_flagged` is the count of cells that each step newly
failed, so a step that flags nothing still records that it ran, which is the
point of an audit log. Note that `n_passed` counts cells of the site-by-sample
matrix, not sites: with 28 sites and 3 samples there are 84 cells, including
those where a sample has no call. A filter cannot fail a call that is absent, so
those cells stay passed and the totals are larger than any per-sample count of
calls.

## The second added slot: qcFilters

The log says which thresholds ran, as text. The `qcFilters` slot keeps the
filter objects themselves: a plain list of `ISNVFilter` objects, in the order
they were applied. The difference is that a stored object can be re-applied to
another experiment, or read programmatically to find out what the strictest
depth threshold was, which is how `calcDiversity()` reports a detection limit
and how `calcSharedVariants()` chooses a depth below which an absence means
nothing. A list in `metadata()` could not be trusted to contain filters at all.
The accessor is `qcFilters(x)`, with the replacement form
`qcFilters(x) <- value`.

```{r object-qcfilters}
qcFilters(example_whe)
length(qcFilters(example_qc))
qcFilters(example_qc)[[1]]
```

The untouched object returns an empty list, `list()`. After one `flagISNV()`
call the list has length one, and its single element prints as the filter that
was used, with every threshold it carried. Had we filtered twice, the list would
have two elements in the order applied, and the later one would not replace the
earlier: both were applied, so both are recorded.

## What subsetting and combining do to the two slots

Only two other operations in the package touch these slots, and both are worth
knowing about before the slots are trusted. Subsetting with `[`, or through
`passedISNV()`, keeps `qcLog` and `qcFilters` unchanged: the log still describes
the object it was written on, so after a subset its `n_passed` can exceed the
number of cells in hand. `combineRows()` and `combineCols()` go the other way
and concatenate the logs and the filter lists of their arguments, so a combined
object carries every step that any part of it went through, in order.

```{r object-slots-subset}
part <- example_qc[1:5, ]
qcLog(part)$n_passed
nrow(part) * ncol(part)
length(qcFilters(combineRows(example_qc[1:5, ], example_qc[6:10, ])))
```

The log of the five-site subset still reports 75 passing cells, counted over the
84 cells of the full object, against the 15 cells the subset holds: the log is a
history, not a summary of the current object. The combined object, built from
two subsets of the same filtered object, carries two filters, one inherited from
each part, which is the faithful record even though both are the same filter
applied once.

## What the validity method enforces

An S4 validity method runs when an object is constructed and whenever
`validObject()` is called on it, and refuses a malformed object. For this class
it enforces four things: that `qcLog` has the six columns named above; that
`qcFilters` holds only `ISNVFilter` objects; that an `altFreq` assay exists
whenever the object has any assay at all; and that a `qcPass` assay, if present,
is a logical matrix. The replacement forms `qcLog(x) <-` and `qcFilters(x) <-`
assign the slot without re-checking, so a malformed object can exist until
something looks at it, which is why the chunk below calls `validObject()` on the
two it builds. The reason to check these invariants is that every downstream
function assumes them, and an assumption that fails quietly fails somewhere far
from its cause. The chunk provokes three of the four failures with `try()`, so
that the vignette continues after each error.

```{r object-validity}
gr <- GRanges("seg", IRanges::IRanges(1:3, width = 1))
try(WithinHostExperiment(
    assays = list(altFreq = matrix(c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3), ncol = 1),
                  qcPass = matrix(c(1L, 1L, 0L), ncol = 1)),
    rowRanges = gr,
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(sample_id = "S1")))
bad_filters <- example_whe
qcFilters(bad_filters) <- list("minDepth = 100")
try(validObject(bad_filters))
bad_log <- example_whe
qcLog(bad_log) <- qcLog(example_whe)[, c("step", "parameter")]
try(validObject(bad_log))
```

Each message names the invariant that was broken. The first rejects a `qcPass`
matrix of integers: `1L` and `0L` would be read as `TRUE` and `FALSE` in some
places and as counts in others, so the class refuses the ambiguity rather than
resolving it. The second rejects a character string where an `ISNVFilter`
belongs, which is what stops a hand-written note from being mistaken later for a
filter that was applied. The third rejects a log whose last four columns have
been dropped, naming all four. The fourth invariant, the required `altFreq`
assay, is caught by the constructor itself with a message that lists the assays
you did supply.

## Converting to other containers

An object that cannot be handed to another tool is a dead end, so two coercions
are provided. `as(x, "data.frame")` gives one row per site and sample that has
an observed frequency, which is the shape that `ggplot2`, `dplyr` and base R
modelling expect. `as(x, "VRanges")` gives the same rows as a `VRanges`, the
variant-centric container of `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("VariantAnnotation")`, whose
reference, alternative and depth fields are named as that ecosystem expects.

```{r object-coerce}
head(as(example_whe, "data.frame"), 4)
as(example_whe, "VRanges")
```

The data frame carries the coordinates, the alleles, the sample identifier and
one column per assay, so the `NA` cells of the matrix form simply do not appear
as rows. The `VRanges` summary reports the number of ranges, which again is the
number of calls rather than the number of sites, and names its fields
`refDepth`, `altDepth` and `totalDepth`. Its final line reports no `seqlengths`,
so the recorded genome length does not survive this conversion; compute per-site
quantities before converting, or record the length again on the result.

# Importing calls

## From VCF files

A variant caller writes one file per sample, and nothing in that file says which
host the sample came from, whether it is a replicate, or which other sample it
should be paired with. `readWithinHost()` therefore takes the files and the
sample table together, so that the object cannot exist without its metadata. One
file corresponds to one sample; a file holding several samples is read with
`VariantAnnotation::readVcf()` and converted, as shown next.

Two arguments repay attention. `caller` names the field layout, because callers
record the same quantities under different names: iVar-style files carry
`ALT_FREQ`, `ALT_DP` and `REF_DP`, LoFreq carries `AF` and `DP` in the INFO
column, Freebayes carries `AO`, `RO` and `DP`. The default `"auto"` reads the
header's `##source` line and chooses. `genome` takes the reference sequence as a
`DNAStringSet`, from which the length of each sequence is recorded in
`seqlengths()`; a header carrying `##contig` lines records it without help. This
is why `calcDiversity()` never asks you for a genome length, and why the
functions that do take one, `calcNeutralityTests()` and `buildSFS()`, can be
handed `sum(seqlengths(x))` rather than a typed number, as every chunk below
does.

```{r import-vcf}
vcf1 <- system.file("extdata", "test_donor.vcf",
    package = "WithinHostExperiment")
vcf2 <- system.file("extdata", "test_recipient.vcf",
    package = "WithinHostExperiment")
ref <- Biostrings::readDNAStringSet(
    system.file("extdata", "test_ref.fa", package = "WithinHostExperiment"))
whe <- readWithinHost(
    c(vcf1, vcf2),
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(
        sample_id = c("donor", "recipient"),
        host_id   = c("P1", "P2"),
        role      = c("donor", "recipient"),
        pair_id   = c("pair_1", "pair_1")
    ),
    caller = "ivar",
    genome = ref
)
whe
GenomeInfoDb::seqlengths(whe)
```

The object has 20 variant sites and 2 samples. Twenty is the union of the
positions the two callers reported, not the number of calls: a position reported
in only one sample still becomes a row, with `NA` in the other column. The
`qcLog` line reads zero steps, as it must straight after import, and one
transmission pair has been recognised from the `role` and `pair_id` columns we
supplied. The `seqlengths()` call confirms that the 1,000-base length of the
reference has been recorded. If that line had returned `NA`, the per-site
indices later in this vignette would stop with instructions rather than divide
by a number nobody chose.

## From a VCF already read into R

Sometimes the file is already in memory, because it has been filtered, or
because it holds several samples and so cannot be passed to `readWithinHost()`
directly. The coercion `as(vcf, "WithinHostExperiment")` converts a
`CollapsedVCF` or `ExpandedVCF` object, choosing the field layout from the
header exactly as `caller = "auto"` does, and taking every sample the file
holds. Sequence lengths recorded in the file are kept.

```{r import-vcf-coerce}
v <- VariantAnnotation::readVcf(vcf1)
as(v, "WithinHostExperiment")
```

The result has 15 sites and 1 sample, which is the donor file on its own; the 20
rows above were the union across two files. No transmission pair is reported,
because this route has no sample table to read a `role` column from: the sample
names come from the VCF, and any other metadata has to be added to `colData()`
afterwards. Records carrying several alternative alleles are split into one row
per allele before conversion, and the import stops rather than guess when the
header declares a per-allele field in a way that would silently give every
allele the first allele's value.

## From an iVar table

`ivar variants` writes a tab-separated table, not a VCF, so an iVar-style VCF
has been through a converter. `readWithinHostTable()` reads the table directly,
which avoids that conversion. It accepts iVar's own columns (`REGION`, `POS`,
`REF`, `ALT`, `REF_DP`, `ALT_DP`, `ALT_FREQ`, `TOTAL_DP`) with
`format = "ivar"`, and a generic layout (`chrom`, `pos`, `ref`, `alt`, `aaf`,
`depth`) with `format = "generic"`.

```{r import-tsv}
tsv <- system.file("extdata", "test_donor_ivar.tsv",
    package = "WithinHostExperiment")
whe_tsv <- readWithinHostTable(tsv, format = "ivar")
whe_tsv
GenomeInfoDb::seqlengths(whe_tsv)
```

The object again has 15 sites and 1 sample, and no sample table was supplied, so
the sample identifier was taken from the file name. The important line is the
last one: `seqlengths()` returns `NA`, because a table carries no reference and
no header. Nothing is wrong with the object, but the per-site indices will
refuse to run until the length is recorded, with
`GenomeInfoDb::seqlengths(x) <- c(name = length)`. The worked example on real
data does exactly that.

# Quality control

Within-host calls are noisy, and the noise is concentrated where the signal is.
Roder et al. (2023) found that the choice of variant caller and the use of
replicate sequencing had the largest effects on which iSNVs were discovered. The
package addresses both: it harmonises the output of several callers on import,
and it treats replicate concordance as a first-class quality-control step rather
than a script.

The design principle throughout is **flag, do not delete**. A quality-control
step sets entries of the logical `qcPass` matrix to `FALSE`, which we call a
**QC flag**, and records itself in `qcLog`. No row is removed, so the same
object can be re-examined under a different threshold, and the reason each call
was set aside is still readable.

## Describing a filter

An `ISNVFilter` is a small object holding the thresholds, separate from the act
of applying them, so that the same thresholds can be applied to several
experiments and stored on each. Six thresholds are carried: `minDepth`, a floor
on read depth; `minFreq`, the **detection threshold**, the lowest allele
frequency a call may have and be kept; `maxFreq`, above which a variant is
treated as a consensus-level change rather than within-host variation;
`minAltReads`, a floor on the reads supporting the alternative allele;
`maxStrandBias`, the largest tolerated fold-difference between the strands; and
`replicateConc`, recorded for provenance but applied by a separate function.
Defaults follow the within-host literature, and the class documentation gives
the reasoning for each.

```{r qc-filter}
filt <- ISNVFilter(minDepth = 200L, minFreq = 0.03)
filt
```

The `show` method prints every threshold, including the four we did not set,
which is the point of printing it: `minFreq` and `maxFreq` appear as the
interval `[0.03, 0.5]`, so a call at 60% is excluded here as a near-fixed
change, not retained. A threshold you did not think about is still a threshold
that will be applied, so read this output before trusting a filtered object.
Base and mapping quality are deliberately absent: the object holds no per-site
quality score, so those belong in the variant caller.

## Applying a filter

`flagISNV()` applies the thresholds in order and returns a new object. Nothing
is deleted; the `qcPass` matrix and the `qcLog` change. Reading the log
afterwards is how you learn which threshold did the work, which is rarely the
one expected.

```{r qc-flag}
whe_qc <- flagISNV(whe, filt)
qcLog(whe_qc)
```

Four steps were recorded, one per applicable threshold, with strand bias absent
because this object has no per-strand count assays. The depth filter flagged one
cell and the other three flagged none, so the depth floor of 200 is doing all
the filtering here. `n_passed` settles at 39 out of 40: the matrix is 20 sites
by 2 samples, and the 15 cells where a sample made no call are counted as
passed, because a filter cannot fail an absent call. Do not read `n_passed` as a
number of surviving calls; the next function reports that.

## Summarising quality per sample

`qcSummary()` counts calls rather than cells, one row per sample, and is the
table to report. `total_sites` is the number of sites where that sample has a
frequency, `passed_sites` and `flagged_sites` split them by `qcPass`,
`pass_rate` is the ratio, and `median_depth` and `median_freq` describe the
calls the sample made.

```{r qc-summary}
qcSummary(whe_qc)
```

The donor made 15 calls, of which 14 passed and one was flagged, giving a pass
rate of 0.93; the recipient made 10 and kept all of them. The median depths,
1,600 and 1,950 reads, are what make a 3% frequency threshold meaningful at all:
at that depth 3% is about 50 supporting reads. A pass rate near zero, or a
median depth of a few dozen, means the thresholds and the data disagree, and the
thresholds are usually not the thing to change. These are synthetic files, so
the figures describe the fixture only.

## Extracting the calls that passed

Analysis functions read `qcPass` themselves and use only passing calls by
default, so subsetting is usually unnecessary. When you do need a smaller
object, for example to pass to a function outside the package, `passedISNV()`
keeps every site at which *at least one* sample passed.

```{r qc-passed}
clean <- passedISNV(whe_qc)
cat("Before:", nrow(whe_qc), "sites; after passedISNV:", nrow(clean), "sites\n")
```

The row count does not change here, from 20 sites to 20, which surprises people.
The one flagged call is in the donor at a site where the recipient has no call;
the site is therefore still passed in at least one column, by the rule above,
and the row stays. A site disappears only when every sample's call at it has
been flagged. If you want to remove the flagged *cells* as well, set them to
`NA` in the assays yourself, and expect to justify it: that is the deletion this
package exists to avoid.

## Technology-specific defaults

A **technical replicate** aside, the error profile of the sequencing platform is
the other thing that should set thresholds, and a 3% frequency threshold that is
reasonable for Illumina is not reasonable for a platform whose per-base error
rate is 3%. `adaptiveFilter()` returns a filter with thresholds chosen for a
platform: Illumina, Oxford Nanopore, PacBio HiFi, or a generic fallback. The
documentation gives the measurement behind each number.

```{r qc-adaptive}
adaptiveFilter("illumina")
adaptiveFilter("ont")
adaptiveFilter("pacbio_hifi")
```

The three differ in exactly the ways the platforms differ. Illumina keeps the 3%
threshold at a depth of 100. Nanopore raises the frequency threshold to 10%,
lowers the depth floor to 60, about the depth above which Bull et al. (2020)
reported over 99% sensitivity and precision for single-nucleotide variants, and
sets `maxStrandBias` to `Inf`, which disables strand-bias filtering rather than
apply a threshold nobody has tested. PacBio HiFi sits between the two, at 5% and
a depth of 50. These are starting points for your own data, not results: if you
have replicates, measure your own noise floor instead.

## Replicate-aware quality control

Sequencing the same library twice is the most direct way to find out which
low-frequency calls are real. A **technical replicate** is a second sequencing
of the same biological sample, so a genuine variant should appear at a similar
frequency in both, while an artefact of amplification or base calling need not.
`flagReplicateDiscordance()` compares the frequencies within each
`replicate_group` and flags the sites that disagree by more than
`freqTolerance`; with `requireBothDetected = TRUE` it also flags sites seen in
only one replicate. Flags are applied to every sample of the group, since
discordance is a property of the site rather than of one replicate.

```{r qc-replicate}
rep1 <- system.file("extdata", "test_donor_rep1.vcf",
    package = "WithinHostExperiment")
rep2 <- system.file("extdata", "test_donor_rep2.vcf",
    package = "WithinHostExperiment")
whe_rep <- readWithinHost(
    c(rep1, rep2),
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(
        sample_id       = c("rep1", "rep2"),
        replicate_group = c("donor_reps", "donor_reps"),
        replicate_id    = c("1", "2")
    ),
    caller = "ivar", genome = ref
)
whe_rep <- flagReplicateDiscordance(whe_rep, freqTolerance = 0.05)
qcLog(whe_rep)
```

Two rows are recorded, one per argument, but only the first counts anything: the
function makes a single pass that applies both criteria together and writes the
whole count against `freqTolerance`, while the `requireBothDetected` row records
the setting with `n_flagged` fixed at zero. So the zero in the second row is
structural, and nothing about the data can be read from it. The 6 flagged cells
are three sites across the two replicates: two whose frequencies differ by more
than 0.05, and one that was detected in only one replicate, which the fixture
includes on purpose. A tolerance in percentage points is itself a modelling
choice: the sampling spread of a frequency difference grows with frequency, so a
fixed tolerance removes proportionally more calls at intermediate frequencies
than at the bottom of the range. Report the tolerance alongside any count of
discordant sites.

## Masking primer sites

Amplicon protocols amplify the genome in overlapping pieces, and a read that
begins inside a primer carries the primer's bases rather than the template's. A
**primer site** is therefore a region where an apparent variant may be an
artefact of the protocol, and it is masked rather than interpreted.
`flagPrimerSites()` takes the primer coordinates as a `GRanges`, which is what
`rtracklayer::import.bed()` returns for a BED file, and flags every call inside
them.

```{r qc-primer}
primers <- GRanges("test_segment",
    IRanges::IRanges(start = c(40, 880), end = c(65, 950)))
whe_primer <- flagPrimerSites(whe_qc, primers)
qcLog(whe_primer)
```

The log now has five rows: the four from `flagISNV()` and one `primer_filter`
step recording that two primer regions flagged 6 further cells, leaving 33 of
the 40 cells passing. Because the step is appended rather than replacing
anything, the order in which quality control was applied stays readable. The
number of regions, not their coordinates, is recorded, so keep the BED file with
the analysis.

## Strand bias

**Strand bias** means that the reads supporting a variant come overwhelmingly
from one strand. Since a real variant is present on both strands of the
template, strong bias suggests a systematic error. The simple fold-difference
used by `flagISNV()` works for data with balanced strand coverage, but amplicon
data are unbalanced by construction, and Mostefai et al. (2024) showed that
filters ignoring that imbalance discard genuine variants. `sciStrandBias()`
therefore normalises each site's forward-to-reverse ratio of alternative reads
by the forward-to-reverse ratio of total coverage summed over all sites, after
adding a pseudocount of one to each of the four counts, and reports the result
on a base-2 logarithmic scale: zero means a site as balanced as the data as a
whole.

```{r qc-sci}
sci <- sciStrandBias(
    fwd_alt   = c(50, 2, 30),
    rev_alt   = c(45, 40, 28),
    fwd_total = c(500, 500, 500),
    rev_total = c(480, 480, 480))
sci
```

The first and third sites score 0.09 and 0.04, within a hair of balance. The
second scores -3.83, meaning its alternative reads are about 2 to the power
3.83, roughly fourteenfold, scarcer on the forward strand than the global
coverage ratio would predict; 2 forward reads against 40 reverse is the
signature of a strand-specific artefact. Scores are not p-values, and the
threshold is a judgement: `flagStrandBiasSCI()` applies `|SCI| > maxSCI` to an
object carrying the four per-strand count assays, with `maxSCI = 1.5` by
default.

## Detecting cross-contamination

In pooled sequencing, adapters are occasionally exchanged between library
molecules, so reads from one sample are assigned to another. The signature is
distinctive: a variant at high frequency in one sample appears at a very low
frequency in another sample from the same run, at a ratio consistent with the
hopping rate rather than with biology. `detectCrossContamination()` looks for
that pattern and returns the suspect pairs, one row per event, without flagging
anything.

```{r qc-contamination}
gr_c <- GRanges("seg", IRanges::IRanges(c(100, 200, 300), width = 1))
mcols(gr_c)$ref <- c("A", "C", "G")
mcols(gr_c)$alt <- c("T", "G", "A")
freq_c <- matrix(c(0.80, 0.05, 0.30, 0.01, 0.40, 0.00), nrow = 3, ncol = 2)
whe_c <- WithinHostExperiment(
    assays = list(altFreq = freq_c), rowRanges = gr_c,
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(sample_id = c("A", "B"),
        run = c("run1", "run1")))
detectCrossContamination(whe_c, runCol = "run")
```

Two events are reported, and the column to read is `freq_ratio`, the sink
frequency over the source frequency. The first event, position 100 at 80% in
sample A and 1% in sample B, has a ratio of 0.0125, within the 0.1% to 2% range
typical of index hopping on Illumina platforms, so it is a plausible
contaminant. The second, at 0.125, is several times the upper end of that range
and is more likely a genuine shared variant. The function suggests; it does not
decide, and a real study would set its own criteria on this table.

## Putting the steps together

Every function in the package takes the object as its first argument, so steps
compose with R's native pipe, and the composed pipeline reads in the order it
runs. This is also the shape in which quality control actually removes rows,
since the masking and the extraction happen together.

```{r qc-pipe}
result <- whe |>
    flagISNV(ISNVFilter(minDepth = 200L, minFreq = 0.03)) |>
    flagPrimerSites(primers) |>
    passedISNV()
cat("Input:", nrow(whe), "sites; after QC and primer masking:",
    nrow(result), "sites\n")
```

Twenty sites enter and 17 leave. The three that go are the sites inside the
primer regions where no sample had a passing call left, which is why this
pipeline changes the row count while `passedISNV()` alone did not. The order
matters: flagging after extracting would flag an object from which the evidence
had already been removed, and the log would no longer describe the data in hand.

# Annotation

## Labelling sites with genes

A list of positions says little until each position is attached to a gene, and
the comparison most within-host studies want, which genes carry more variation
than expected, needs that label. `annotateGenes()` adds a `GENE` column to the
row metadata by overlapping the sites with gene ranges. The ranges are supplied
as a `GRanges`, which is what `rtracklayer::import()` returns for a GFF3 or GTF
file; the gene records are the rows with `type == "gene"`. A `TxDb` works too,
and its genes are taken with `GenomicFeatures::genes()`.

The quantity computed is a simple interval overlap, ignoring strand because a
variant site has no strand, with the label taken from the column named by
`nameCol`, by default the GFF3 `Name` attribute. Where genes overlap, the
default keeps the label of the longest overlapping range. Here a two-gene
annotation of the synthetic segment is written to a temporary file and imported,
as a real annotation would be.

```{r annotate-genes}
gff_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".gff3")
writeLines(c(
    "##gff-version 3",
    "test_segment\t.\tgene\t1\t500\t.\t+\t.\tID=gene-A;Name=geneA",
    "test_segment\t.\tgene\t501\t1000\t.\t+\t.\tID=gene-B;Name=geneB"
), gff_file)
features <- rtracklayer::import(gff_file)
genes <- features[features$type == "gene"]
whe_ann <- annotateGenes(whe_qc, genes, nameCol = "Name")
table(mcols(SummarizedExperiment::rowRanges(whe_ann))$GENE, useNA = "ifany")
```

Eleven sites fall in `geneA` and nine in `geneB`, and the absence of an `NA`
column means every site lies inside some gene, as it must when two genes tile
the whole segment. A large `NA` count in real data means either that many sites
are intergenic or that the annotation does not cover the region, and the two are
worth telling apart. One failure mode is handled before the overlap: the
sequence names on the two sides are compared, and the function stops if they
share none. The same reference is often named differently by different sources,
`NC_045512.2` in RefSeq against `MN908947.3` in GenBank for SARS-CoV-2, and an
overlap across mismatched names would otherwise return `NA` everywhere without
any error at all.

## Codon and amino acid consequences

A substitution inside a coding sequence either leaves the amino acid unchanged,
a **synonymous** change, or alters it, a **nonsynonymous** change, with a
**nonsense** change the special case that creates a stop codon. The distinction
is the foundation of every analysis of selection, because selection acts on
proteins: purifying selection removes amino acid changes faster than silent
ones, so the ratio of the two classes is informative where neither count is
informative alone.

`annotateCodonChange()` classifies every single-nucleotide iSNV. It needs the
coding sequences, as the CDS records of an annotation, and the reference
sequence as a `DNAStringSet`, and it passes the sites to
`VariantAnnotation::predictCoding()`, so the translation comes from
Bioconductor's own annotation machinery rather than from a codon table carried
here. CDS records sharing an `ID` are joined into one coding sequence, which is
how a GFF3 file describes a protein split across a ribosomal frameshift. Here
the segment is given one coding sequence covering its first 999 bases.

```{r annotate-codon}
gff_cds <- tempfile(fileext = ".gff3")
writeLines(c("##gff-version 3",
    "test_segment\t.\tCDS\t1\t999\t.\t+\t0\tID=cds-1;gene=testGene"), gff_cds)
cds <- rtracklayer::import(gff_cds)
cds <- cds[cds$type == "CDS"]
whe_codon <- annotateCodonChange(whe_qc, cds, ref)
mc <- mcols(SummarizedExperiment::rowRanges(whe_codon))
table(mc$CONSEQUENCE, useNA = "ifany")
head(as.data.frame(mc[, c("GENEID", "PROTEINLOC", "REFCODON", "VARCODON",
    "REFAA", "VARAA", "CONSEQUENCE")]), 4)
```

The table classifies all 20 sites: 15 nonsynonymous, 3 synonymous and 2
nonsense, with no `NA` because every site here falls inside the coding sequence.
In real data the `NA` class collects sites outside every coding sequence,
insertions and deletions, multi-nucleotide substitutions, and codons holding an
ambiguous base, which are left untranslated with a warning rather than guessed
at. In the per-site columns, `REFCODON` and `VARCODON` are the codon before and
after the substitution, read on the coding sequence's own strand, `REFAA` and
`VARAA` the amino acids they encode, with `*` for a stop codon, and `PROTEINLOC`
the codon's position in the protein. Row 1, `TTC` to `TTT`, keeps phenylalanine
and so is synonymous; row 2, `CAA` to `CAC`, turns glutamine into histidine. The
classes carry no biological meaning here: the segment is a synthetic sequence,
and a fixture with two nonsense changes among twenty sites would be
extraordinary in a real infection. Where coding sequences overlap, as ORF1a and
ORF1ab do in SARS-CoV-2, a site lies in several; the longest is reported by
default and `collapse = "all"` keeps every one.

# Diversity

## How much variation a host carries

Diversity indices compress a host's iSNV frequencies into one number per sample,
which is what makes hosts, timepoints or treatment groups comparable at all. The
compression also loses information, so the index has to be chosen for the
question, and reported with what it rests on.

`calcDiversity()` returns six indices, each treating every site as a biallelic
locus. **Richness** is simply the number of iSNV sites that passed quality
control. **Shannon entropy** is a measure of uncertainty about which allele a
randomly chosen read carries, summed over sites, so it rises both with the
number of sites and with how even the frequencies are. **Nucleotide diversity**,
written pi, is the expected number of differences per site between two genomes
drawn at random from the host, with a finite-sample correction for read depth
following Nei (1987). **Watterson's theta** is a second diversity estimate built
from the number of segregating sites rather than their frequencies, using the
sample's median depth as the sample size. That is the sample size the `tajimaD`
manual page warns against, since reads are not independent lineages and a
depth-sized n makes this theta too small; the neutrality functions cap n at 100
instead, so their Watterson estimate is larger than this column and the two are
not comparable. **Simpson's index** here is the probability that two alleles
drawn at a site differ, summed over sites. **Chao1** estimates the richness that
deeper sequencing would have found, from the numbers of sites whose alternative
allele was seen in exactly one and in exactly two reads; with no doubletons the
bias-corrected form is used, and without an `altCount` assay it simply equals
the richness. The two per-site quantities, pi and Watterson's theta, divide by
the genome length, which the function reads from `seqlengths()`; an object
without a recorded length stops with instructions rather than guess.

```{r diversity}
div <- calcDiversity(whe_qc)
div
```

Each row is one sample, and the first two columns say what the indices rest on.
`n_sites_assessed` is the number of sites at which the sample has any call,
before quality control, and `detection_limit` is the lowest frequency the
filters applied would have let through, here 0.03. Together they let a zero be
read: a pi of zero with a positive `n_sites_assessed` means every call failed
quality control, while a zero with `n_sites_assessed` of zero means no call was
made, and the two call for different actions. In this object the donor's 15
assessed sites leave 14 after filtering, with pi of 4.5 per thousand sites and a
Shannon entropy of 6.84; the recipient's 10 give pi of 3.2 per thousand and
4.92. Chao1 equals the richness in both, because no passing call at these depths
rests on only one or two reads, so there is nothing to add. The donor's
Watterson's theta of 1.8e-03 uses its median depth of 1,600 as the sample size
and is the uncapped value the neutrality section below sets against a capped
one. Shannon entropy and Simpson's index are summed over sites rather than
averaged, so values above 1 are expected and they are not comparable across
genomes of different length. These are synthetic fixtures: 14 iSNVs in 1,000
bases is denser than any real within-host population, and the numbers show the
shape of the output only.

## Checking an estimate for plausibility

A diversity estimate far from the values usually seen for a pathogen is more
often a unit, depth or quality-control problem than a discovery, and the
commonest version of that problem is a per-site quantity that was never divided
by the genome length. `checkDiversityPlausibility()` compares each sample's
estimates against a wide range per pathogen and reports whether each falls
inside it. The ranges are the package's own heuristics, listed on its manual
page and set generously enough that a correctly computed estimate on typical
data falls inside; they are not taken from the literature and they are not a
validation.

```{r diversity-plausibility}
checkDiversityPlausibility(div, pathogen = "sars_cov_2")
```

One row per sample and metric: `observed` is the estimate, `expected_min` and
`expected_max` bound the range, and `in_range` is the verdict. Both samples pass
on Shannon entropy and fail on pi, whose estimates near 4e-03 and 3e-03 sit
above the upper bound of 1e-03 for SARS-CoV-2. That failure is the right answer
for the wrong-looking reason: the fixture is a 1,000-base segment carrying more
than a dozen iSNVs, so its per-site diversity really is far above anything a
coronavirus shows, and the check has caught a fixture, not a bug. On real data a
result like this would send you to the depth distribution and the detection
threshold first. A result inside the range, conversely, says only that nothing
is grossly wrong.

## Modelling diversity across samples

With one index per sample, the question usually becomes whether the index moves
with something: a sampling day, a vaccination status, a treatment group.
`fitDiversityModel()` fits an ordinary linear model with `stats::lm()` and
returns the coefficient table tidied into a data frame, adding a grouping column
as a fixed effect when one is named. Because such a model is usually fitted once
per index, the p-values need correcting for the number of tests, which
`multitestCorrection()` does through `stats::p.adjust()`, defaulting to the
Benjamini and Hochberg procedure. When the grouping is already a column of the
sample table and no model is wanted, `compareDiversity()` computes one index per
sample and applies a Wilcoxon rank-sum test to two groups or a Kruskal-Wallis
test to more; with fewer than two samples in either of two groups it returns
`NA` rather than a test.

```{r diversity-model}
div_df <- data.frame(
    shannon = c(1.2, 1.5, 0.8, 1.1, 1.9, 0.7),
    timepoint = c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3),
    group = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B"))
res <- fitDiversityModel(div_df, shannon ~ timepoint, group_col = "group")
res$summary_df
multitestCorrection(c(0.001, 0.04, 0.03, 0.5))
```

The coefficient table gives an estimate, a standard error, a t value and a
p-value per term. The slope on `timepoint` is -0.20 with a standard error of
0.26, so the data are consistent with no change at all, and the group difference
of 0.07 is far smaller than its own standard error: six hand-written values
cannot show a trend, which is the honest reading. The correction then turns four
raw p-values into adjusted ones, and the two middle values, 0.04 and 0.03, both
become 0.053 and so cross from one side of the conventional 0.05 to the other.
Correcting after choosing which tests to report is not enough; the set of tests
has to be fixed in advance for the adjusted values to mean what they claim.

# Site frequency spectrum

## Building a spectrum

Two hosts can carry the same number of iSNVs at the same average frequency and
still have quite different populations: one may have many rare variants and the
other a few intermediate ones. The **site frequency spectrum** is the
distribution that tells them apart, a histogram of allele frequencies across
sites. It is the quantity the neutrality statistics are computed from, so
building it once and reusing it is both clearer and cheaper than recomputing
summaries separately.

`buildSFS()` constructs a `WithinHostSFS` object for one sample. Two choices
define it. The first is folding. A **folded** spectrum bins the minor allele
frequency, from the detection threshold to 0.5, and so makes no claim about
which allele is ancestral; an **unfolded** spectrum bins the alternative allele
frequency from the threshold to 1, and thereby treats the reference allele as
ancestral at every site. Fold unless you have a reason to believe the reference
is close to the population the host was infected from. The second choice is the
detection threshold, which sets where the first bin starts: below it variants
are unobservable, so starting at zero would invent an empty region of the
spectrum. The genome length is read off the object and passed in, rather than
typed. Unlike the length, the threshold is not read off the object: `buildSFS()`
defaults it to 0.03 whatever filters were applied, so pass `threshold` yourself
to match the `detection_limit` that `calcDiversity()` reports. With the Nanopore
preset's 10% floor, leaving the default would start the spectrum below the
lowest frequency any call could have. `buildSFSList()` takes the same arguments
and returns one spectrum per sample, named by `sample_id`.

```{r sfs-build}
glen <- sum(GenomeInfoDb::seqlengths(whe_qc))
sfs_donor <- buildSFS(whe_qc, sampleIdx = "donor", nBins = 10L,
    genomeLength = glen)
sfs_donor
```

The summary reports 14 variants distributed over 10 bins, which matches the
donor's 14 passing calls, so no call fell outside the binned range.
`folded: TRUE` and `polarization: none` record that this spectrum carries no
claim about ancestry, which is why the statistics needing derived-allele
frequencies will refuse it. The threshold of 0.03 is where the first bin begins,
`corrected: FALSE` says no ascertainment correction has been applied, and the
median depth of 1,600 reads is stored because the binomial correction below
needs it. With 14 variants in 10 bins most bins hold one site or none, so this
spectrum has no shape to speak of; real analyses need hundreds of sites.

## Correcting for what could not be seen

A detection threshold does not merely remove rare variants, it distorts the
shape of the spectrum, because the bins near the threshold are the ones whose
contents are partly unobservable. `correctSFSBias()` reweights the bins to
compensate, by one of two methods. The `"truncation"` method assumes a uniform
density of frequencies and multiplies every bin by the reciprocal of the
observable fraction of the range, which rescales the spectrum without changing
its shape. The `"binomial"` method uses the stored depth to compute the
probability of observing a variant at each bin's frequency, and divides each bin
by that probability, with detectability floored at 0.01 so that no bin is
inflated more than a hundredfold.

```{r sfs-correct}
correctSFSBias(sfs_donor, method = "truncation")
correctSFSBias(sfs_donor, method = "binomial")
```

Both results report `corrected: TRUE` and, here, the same 14 variants as before.
That is the correct answer rather than a failure. The truncation factor is 0.5
divided by 0.5 minus 0.03, about 1.06, and bin counts are whole numbers, so
rounding absorbs the rescaling entirely. The binomial correction changes nothing
for a different reason: at a median depth of 1,600 reads, a variant at 3% is
expected to be supported by about 48 reads, so detectability is essentially 1 in
every bin and there is nothing to inflate. Note that a corrected spectrum no
longer holds raw counts, so its number of segregating sites, and any statistic
computed from it, inherits the correction's assumptions. Use uncorrected spectra
when comparing two of them.

## Comparing two spectra

Asking whether two hosts, two timepoints, or the kept and discarded halves of
one sample's calls have the same spectrum is a question about shape rather than
totals. `compareSFS()` answers it with a chi-squared test for homogeneity on the
raw counts in matching bins. Because the test compares counts bin by bin, the
two spectra must share their breaks, their folding and their polarisation, and
neither may be bias-corrected; the function stops, naming the difference, when
any of this fails.

```{r sfs-compare}
sfs_recip <- buildSFS(whe_qc, sampleIdx = "recipient", nBins = 10L,
    genomeLength = glen)
cmp <- compareSFS(sfs_donor, sfs_recip)
cmp[c("chisq_stat", "df", "chisq_p", "min_expected", "chisq_approx_ok",
    "n1", "n2")]
```

The statistic is 3.57 on 8 degrees of freedom, with a p-value of 0.89: no
evidence that the donor's 14 calls and the recipient's 10 are distributed
differently. The degrees of freedom are 8 rather than 9 because bins empty in
both spectra are dropped before testing, and the top bin holds nothing in
either. The decisive line is `chisq_approx_ok`, which is `FALSE`: the smallest
expected count is 0.42, far below the 5 that the chi-squared approximation
needs, so this p-value should not be quoted. The function reports that condition
instead of warning about it, so that code can check it; a Monte Carlo p-value
from `stats::chisq.test(simulate.p.value = TRUE)` is the usual remedy, and more
sites is the real one.

# Neutrality and selection

## Neutrality statistics from the object

Neutrality statistics ask whether the frequency spectrum looks like the one
expected when every variant is equally fit. They are summaries of spectrum
shape, and in within-host data that is all they should be asked to be.
**Tajima's D** contrasts nucleotide diversity, which weights
intermediate-frequency variants, with Watterson's theta, which counts
segregating sites regardless of frequency, and normalises the difference by its
expected standard deviation (Tajima 1989). Negative values indicate an excess of
rare variants, as purifying selection or a recent expansion would produce;
positive values indicate an excess of intermediate ones. **Fu's Fs** is a second
statistic sensitive to an excess of rare alleles (Fu 1997). One assumption
behind it is worth naming: Fs is defined on the number of distinct haplotypes,
which per-site calls cannot supply, so `fusFs()` takes that number to be one
more than the segregating sites. The package does not phase haplotypes, so
nothing checks this.

`calcNeutralityTests()` computes both per sample. One detail dominates their
interpretation: reads are not independent lineages. Deep sequencing samples a
viral population whose effective size is far smaller than the depth, and using
raw depth as the sample size inflates the harmonic number in Watterson's
estimator and biases D upwards. The method therefore caps the effective sample
size at 100, following Lauring (2020) as the `tajimaD` manual page explains, and
reports `n_sites`, the number of segregating sites each statistic rests on.
Below three segregating sites D is a function of one or two frequencies rather
than of a spectrum, so it is returned as `NA` with a warning.

```{r neutrality-tests}
nt <- calcNeutralityTests(whe_qc, genomeLength = glen)
nt
```

The donor's D is 1.83 on 14 segregating sites and the recipient's 1.78 on 10,
with Fu's Fs of 0.04 for the donor and 0.69 for the recipient; on so few sites
neither value is interpretable. Always read D next to `n_sites`: a D computed
from 10 sites is a description of 10 numbers, not a test. These fixtures are
synthetic, and their frequencies were written by hand across the whole range
from 4% to 45%, which is exactly what produces a positive D, so the sign here is
a property of how the file was written. In real within-host data negative values
are the common case, and negative D is expected both under purifying selection
and after a bottleneck, so the statistic cannot distinguish them. Report D as a
description of the spectrum, not as a test with a p-value.

## Statistics from a spectrum, including Fay and Wu's H

Building the spectrum once and deriving every statistic from it has one further
advantage: it makes room for a statistic that needs more than the folded
spectrum. **Fay and Wu's H** is the difference between nucleotide diversity and
an estimator that weights high-frequency variants heavily, so a *negative* H
marks an excess of high-frequency *derived* variants, the signature of a recent
sweep or of hitchhiking (Fay and Wu 2000), while a positive H means the derived
variants sit mostly at low frequency. It needs to know which allele is derived
at each site, so `neutralityFromSFS()` stops on a folded spectrum and reports
the polarisation it used. On an unfolded spectrum built here, that polarisation
is `"reference"`: the reference allele stands in for the ancestral one, which
holds only as far as the reference resembles the infecting population.

```{r neutrality-sfs}
sfs_unf <- buildSFS(whe_qc, sampleIdx = "donor", nBins = 10L, fold = FALSE,
    genomeLength = glen)
neutralityFromSFS(sfs_unf)
```

The list reports the ingredients as well as the results: 14 segregating sites,
an effective sample size of 100 from the depth cap, pi of 4.3e-03, Watterson's
theta of 2.7e-03, larger than the 1.8e-03 of the diversity table because n is
capped here, and Fay and Wu's theta_H of 2.0e-03 per site, then D of 1.66, Fs of
-0.14 and H of 2.4e-03, with `polarization` recording the assumption. Two
cautions. First, D here is 1.66 while the object-based route above gave 1.83,
for two reasons: this route reconstructs pi from bin midpoints rather than from
the frequencies themselves, and it omits the n/(n-1) finite-sample correction
that the object route applies. The two are not expected to agree to the last
digit, and neither is more correct than the other. Second, H is positive here
because nothing in the fixture is a high-frequency derived variant: with the
reference treated as ancestral, every call lies below 45%, so the high-frequency
bins that would pull theta_H above pi are empty. Nothing in these numbers is
biology.

## Within-host pN/pS

The balance of nonsynonymous to synonymous iSNVs inside one host is the most
direct within-host signal of selection, but the raw counts cannot be compared: a
genome offers many more positions at which a substitution would change the amino
acid than positions at which it would not. `pNpSWithinHost()` therefore divides
each count by the number of sites of its own class, counted by the method of Nei
and Gojobori (1986), under which each codon carries three sites divided between
the classes according to how many of its possible substitutions keep the amino
acid. Writing n_S and n_N for the counts and S and N for the sites, the ratio is
(n_N / N) divided by (n_S / S).

This ratio is **pN/pS**, a ratio of *polymorphism* within one host, and it is
not the **dN/dS** of a comparison between two sequences. The distinction is not
pedantry: dN/dS counts substitutions that have fixed between lineages and is
usually corrected for multiple hits at one site, whereas these variants
segregate at a few percent inside one host, where no multiple-hit correction
applies. Under the counting model's assumptions, that every substitution is
equally likely and that there is no selection, pN/pS is expected near 1, and
values below 1 are what purifying selection against amino acid changes produces.

```{r selection-pnps}
pnps <- pNpSWithinHost(whe_qc, cds, ref)
pnps[, c("sample_id", "nS", "nN", "S_sites", "N_sites", "pNpS")]
```

Each row here is one sample, because the fixture has a single gene; in general
the table carries one row per sample and gene, with the per-gene counts, sites
and ratio in six `gene_*` columns that this selection leaves out. The donor
carries 3 synonymous and 11 nonsynonymous iSNVs, the recipient 1 and 9, with
nonsense changes counted as nonsynonymous, and each iSNV counts once whatever
its frequency. `S_sites` and `N_sites`, 219.3 and 725.7, are the same for both
samples because they are a property of the coding sequence, not of the data, and
they sum to 945, three times the 315 sense codons of this 999-base coding
sequence; the other 18 codons are stop codons, which carry no sites of either
class. The ratios, 1.11 and 2.72, must be read with their counts and never
alone: the recipient's ratio rests on a single synonymous iSNV, and one more
such call would roughly halve it. Report pN/pS with n_S and n_N always. The
segment is synthetic, so these values carry no biological meaning; the package's
own figures on real SARS-CoV-2 data give a pooled ratio of 0.29 from 50
nonsynonymous and 49 synonymous calls, which is the order of magnitude a real
within-host estimate has.

## Consensus sequences for between-host comparison

If pN/pS describes polymorphism inside a host, the matching between-host
quantity is dN/dS between the hosts' consensus sequences. A **consensus
sequence** is the reference with each of a sample's substitutions at or above a
frequency written in, so that it represents the single most common genome in
that host. `consensusSequences()` builds one per sample and returns them as a
`DNAStringSet`. Only substitutions are written in: insertions and deletions are
skipped, with a warning, so that every consensus keeps the reference's length
and stays aligned to the reference and to every other sample, which is what a
codon-aware distance needs.

```{r selection-consensus}
cons <- consensusSequences(whe_qc, ref)
S4Vectors::mcols(cons)
```

The `n_substitutions` column reports how many substitutions were written into
each sequence, and here it is zero for both samples. That is correct: the
default `minFreq` is 0.5, and the highest frequency anywhere in this fixture is
0.45, so no variant is the majority allele at its position and both consensuses
equal the reference. This is the normal situation for within-host data, where
most iSNVs are minority variants, and it is the reason a consensus sequence
throws away almost everything this package measures.

To have two sequences that differ at all, we must lower the threshold far below
0.5, which no real analysis should do: the result is not a consensus but the
reference with every minority variant written in. We do it here only so that the
interface to `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("MSA2dist")` can be shown. The `region`
argument restricts the output to the coding sequence, since a codon-aware model
needs a sequence whose length is a multiple of three and whose frame is known.

```{r selection-kaks, message=FALSE}
cds_region <- GRanges("test_segment", IRanges::IRanges(1, 999), strand = "+")
cons_cds <- consensusSequences(whe_qc, ref, minFreq = 0.03, region = cds_region)
if (requireNamespace("MSA2dist", quietly = TRUE)) {
    kaks <- cons_cds |> MSA2dist::dnastring2kaks(model = "Li")
    kaks[, c("seq1", "seq2", "Ka", "Ks", "Ka/Ks")]
}
```

One row is returned per pair of sequences. `Ka` and `Ks` are the nonsynonymous
and synonymous distances per site under Li's model, 1.5e-02 and 5.6e-03, and
their ratio, 2.70, is what the `Ka/Ks` column holds; `Ka/Ks` is this
literature's name for dN/dS. These numbers measure nothing: the sequences differ
only because we wrote in variants at 3%, so the comparison is between two
artefacts of a threshold, on a synthetic segment. What the chunk does show is
the division of labour. Polymorphism within a host is `pNpSWithinHost()`;
divergence between sequences is a multiple-sequence-alignment problem, and
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("MSA2dist")` implements the published models for it, so
this package produces the sequences rather than reimplementing the distances.

## Selection coefficients from a trajectory

When the same host is sampled repeatedly, a variant's frequency trajectory
carries more information than any single-timepoint ratio. Under a deterministic
model of selection, the logit of the frequency, the logarithm of p over 1 minus
p, is linear in time with slope equal to the selection coefficient s.
`estimateSelectionCoefficient()` returns one estimate of s per consecutive
interval, scaled by the generation time, so that the estimates can be compared
and their variability seen.

```{r selection-coefficient}
freqs <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50)
s_hat <- estimateSelectionCoefficient(freqs, times = c(0, 3, 7, 14))
s_hat
```

Three estimates come back for four timepoints, 0.249, 0.275 and 0.157 per day,
one per interval. The first two agree and the third is about half as large,
which is what a variant whose rise is slowing looks like; averaging them would
hide exactly the information the per-interval output preserves. The model is
deterministic, so it treats all of the change as selection and none as drift,
and at these frequencies in a within-host population drift is not negligible.
Read these values as a description of the trajectory's steepness, and see the
section on scope for what a drift-aware analysis would need.

# Transmission

## Finding the pairs

A **transmission pair** is two samples from different hosts, one of whom is
believed to have infected the other, labelled `donor` and `recipient`. The
pairing is epidemiological knowledge that no sequence analysis can supply, so it
is declared in `colData()` through the `role` and `pair_id` columns, and the
analysis functions read it from there rather than taking donor and recipient as
arguments. `transmissionPairs()` reports what they will find.

```{r transmission-pairs}
transmissionPairs(whe_qc)
```

One pair is reported, with the donor's and recipient's `sample_id` values and
the `pair_id` that joins them. An empty table means that the pairing is not
expressed in `colData()`, usually because `role` is missing or spelled
differently, and every transmission function will then report that it cannot
find the pair. If a direction is not established, as is often the case, say so
in the text: nothing in the object records how the direction was decided.

## Counting shared variants

The first question about a pair is how many of the donor's iSNVs reached the
recipient. `calcSharedVariants()` counts, over the calls that passed quality
control, the sites present in both hosts, in the donor alone and in the
recipient alone. The subtlety is in the donor-only count. A donor variant absent
from the recipient is evidence of loss in transmission only where the recipient
was sequenced deeply enough at that site to have shown it, so the count is split
three ways by the recipient's depth: adequate, low, or unknown.

```{r transmission-shared}
sv <- calcSharedVariants(whe_qc, pairId = "pair_1")
cat("Shared:", sv$n_shared, "| donor-only:", sv$n_donor_only,
    "| recipient-only:", sv$n_recipient_only, "\n")
cat("Donor-only at adequate / low / unknown recipient depth:",
    sv$n_donor_only_adequate_depth, "/", sv$n_donor_only_low_depth, "/",
    sv$n_donor_only_unknown_depth, "\n")
```

Five sites are shared, nine are donor-only and five recipient-only, 19 in all,
which is the union of the donor's 14 and the recipient's 10 passing calls. Every
one of the nine donor-only sites falls in the unknown-depth group, and that is
the output to attend to. These objects were read from VCF files, which list only
the positions a caller reported, so the recipient's depth at the positions it
did not report is simply not recorded, and no absence here can be distinguished
from a failure to look. A depth matrix from a coverage file, or a table listing
every assessed position, would move these sites into the first two groups and
make the sharing rate interpretable. Until then, report the split, not just the
total.

## A quick bottleneck estimate

A transmission **bottleneck** is the number of viral genomes that founded the
infection in the recipient, written Nb. It matters because it governs how much
of the donor's variation can survive transmission at all: a bottleneck of one or
two makes the recipient's population a near-copy of one donor genome, so most
donor iSNVs are lost by chance rather than by selection. `quickBottleneck()`
computes an approximate beta-binomial maximum likelihood estimate over a grid of
candidate sizes, in the manner of Sobel Leonard et al. (2017), without modelling
the recipient's read depth.

```{r transmission-quick}
nb <- quickBottleneck(whe_qc, pairId = "pair_1", maxNb = 50L)
cat("Nb:", nb$Nb, "with 95% CI [", nb$ci[1], ",", nb$ci[2], "],",
    nb$n_variants, "donor variants, log-likelihood", round(nb$loglik, 2), "\n")
```

The estimate is 3, with a 95% interval from 1 to 7 from 14 donor variants. Three
numbers decide whether to believe such an estimate. `n_variants` is the whole of
the evidence: 14 sites cannot distinguish a bottleneck of 3 from one of 7, which
is what the interval says. The interval's upper end must be well below `maxNb`,
since an estimate that reaches the grid's edge is censored by the grid rather
than supported by the data; `quickBottleneck()` issues no warning, so check
`nb$ci[2]` against `maxNb` yourself, while `exactBottleneck()` warns, but only
when the point estimate itself reaches `maxNb`. And the log-likelihood is only
comparable between estimators run on the same sites.

One further caution applies to every estimator in this section. The frequency
table they work from records a recipient frequency of zero wherever the
recipient made no call, so each of the nine donor-only sites that
`calcSharedVariants()` placed in the unknown-depth group is scored here as a
variant lost in transmission. Where the recipient was simply not sequenced
deeply enough at those positions, that scoring pulls the estimate downwards.
This is a synthetic pair, so 3 is not an estimate of anything.

## Estimators that model depth

`exactBottleneck()` offers three estimators beyond the approximate one.
`"exact_bb"` is a beta-binomial likelihood over the number of transmitted
variant virions that does model the recipient's finite read depth, with two
departures from the published method, both stated on its manual page: when all
or none of the transmitted virions carry the variant, the recipient's read
counts are modelled with a fixed error probability of half the detection
threshold, and the recipient's detection threshold is not integrated out.
`"presence_absence"` uses only whether each donor variant was detected in the
recipient, through the probability 1 minus (1 minus frequency) to the power Nb,
which discards the recipient's frequencies and so is robust to their being
poorly estimated. `"wright_fisher"` is a heuristic score rather than a
likelihood, and says so with a message when it runs. The presence-absence
estimator is shown here because it needs the least from the data.

```{r transmission-exact}
nb_pa <- exactBottleneck(whe_qc, pairId = "pair_1", maxNb = 50L,
    method = "presence_absence")
cat("Presence-absence Nb:", nb_pa$Nb, "with 95% CI [", nb_pa$ci[1], ",",
    nb_pa$ci[2], "] from", nb_pa$n_variants, "variants\n")
```

This estimator returns 2, with an interval from 1 to 4, against the 3 and 1 to 7
above, from the same 14 variants. The two intervals overlap heavily, which is
the expected relationship between estimators using the same sites and different
amounts of each site's information: they are not independent estimates to be
averaged, and the difference between them measures the influence of the
frequency information rather than any uncertainty about Nb. Choose the estimator
that matches what your data support, report which one, and report its interval.

## Exporting for other tools

Bottleneck estimation is a field of its own, and the right move is usually to
hand the data to a dedicated package rather than to re-estimate here.
`asViralBottleneckInput()` writes the donor and recipient frequencies of one
pair into a single frame, which is the input a beta-binomial estimator needs,
and `exportPairFrequencies()` gives the fuller table with coordinates, alleles
and a shared indicator for every site of the pair.

```{r transmission-export}
head(asViralBottleneckInput(whe_qc, pairId = "pair_1"), 4)
head(exportPairFrequencies(whe_qc, pairId = "pair_1"), 4)
```

The first table has three columns, position and the two frequencies, with a zero
where the recipient made no call; a beta-binomial estimator needs no more. The
second keeps `chrom`, `ref` and `alt` as well, so that sites can be matched
across objects by allele rather than by position alone, and flags with `shared`
whether both hosts carry a frequency; here `NA` marks the sites one host did not
report, which the first table renders as zero. Note that the `ViralBottleneck`
package (Zheng et al. 2025) builds its objects from per-base read counts through
`CreateTransmissionObject()`, so prepare those from the `altCount` and
`refCount` assays rather than from either of these frames.

# Longitudinal data

## Tracking frequencies over time

A host sampled once gives a snapshot; a host sampled repeatedly shows which
variants are rising, which are falling and which appear once and vanish. The
functions in this section need two `colData()` columns, a host identifier and a
timepoint, and they work within each host. `trackFrequency()` reshapes the
frequency matrix into the long format such analyses need, one row per variant
and timepoint.

```{r longitudinal-track}
gr_l <- GRanges("seg1", IRanges::IRanges(c(100, 200), width = 1))
mcols(gr_l)$ref <- c("A", "C")
mcols(gr_l)$alt <- c("T", "G")
freq_l <- matrix(c(0.02, 0.10, 0.12, 0.15), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
whe_l <- WithinHostExperiment(
    assays = list(altFreq = freq_l), rowRanges = gr_l,
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(
        sample_id = c("t1", "t2"), host_id = c("H1", "H1"),
        timepoint = c(1, 2)))
trackFrequency(whe_l)
```

Four rows come back for two variants at two timepoints. `variant_key` identifies
a variant as `chrom:pos:alt`, so the same variant is recognisable across
timepoints even though each is a separate column of the matrix, and `qc_passed`
carries the flag forward so that a trajectory can be drawn with the failing
points marked rather than silently dropped. A variant with no call at a
timepoint contributes no row, which is why a trajectory with gaps is not the
same as one that went to zero.

## Detecting emerging variants

Among the trajectories, the interesting ones are those that rise.
`detectEmergingVariants()` reports a variant as emerging when it was below
`freqThreshold` at one timepoint and rose by at least `minIncrease` by the next,
within one host. The defaults, 0.05 for both, mean a variant that starts below
5% and gains at least 5 percentage points.

```{r longitudinal-emerging}
detectEmergingVariants(whe_l)
```

One of the two variants qualifies: the site at position 100 rose from 0.02 to
0.12, a change of 0.10, and the other began at 0.10, above the threshold, so it
is not reported as emerging however much it rose. One row is one *interval*, not
one variant, so a variant that rises twice appears twice, and the output should
be read as a list of intervals to inspect. Neither threshold has any statistical
content: a rise from 2% to 12% at a depth of 50 reads is four reads against six
and no rise at all, so check the depth of each reported interval before taking
it seriously.

## Flagging temporally inconsistent sites

A genuine within-host variant arises from replication and should persist across
consecutive samples, or change smoothly. A variant seen at one timepoint at 5%
and absent at every other is more likely an artefact of library preparation or
base calling. `flagTemporalInconsistency()` classifies each site within each
host as persistent or transient, flags the transient ones, and records the step
in the log. A site is persistent when it is detected at `minTimepoints`
timepoints, optionally requiring them to be consecutive. Note what this cannot
distinguish: a site also goes undetected on a day when its depth was too low or
its frequency left the detection window, so a variant that goes to fixation can
look transient.

```{r longitudinal-temporal}
gr_t <- GRanges("seg1", IRanges::IRanges(c(100, 200, 300), width = 1))
mcols(gr_t)$ref <- c("A", "C", "G")
mcols(gr_t)$alt <- c("T", "G", "A")
freq_t <- matrix(c(0.1, 0.05, 0.15, NA, NA, 0.2, 0.2, NA, 0.1),
    nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
whe_t <- WithinHostExperiment(
    assays = list(altFreq = freq_t), rowRanges = gr_t,
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(
        sample_id = c("t1", "t2", "t3"), host_id = c("H1", "H1", "H1"),
        timepoint = c(1, 2, 3)))
whe_t <- flagTemporalInconsistency(whe_t, minTimepoints = 2L)
mcols(SummarizedExperiment::rowRanges(whe_t))$temporal_class
qcLog(whe_t)
```

The classification reads persistent, transient, persistent: the second site was
detected only at the first timepoint, while the first and third were seen at two
or three. The log then records one step that flagged 3 cells, which is the one
transient site across all three samples of this host, since the classification
is a property of the site in that host and the flag follows it. With several
hosts, a site transient in one and persistent in another is flagged only in the
samples of the first, and the site-level class reads persistent. The flag is an
invitation to review, not a verdict.

# Several callers

## Building a consensus call set

When replicates are unavailable, the next best check on a low-frequency call is
whether a second variant caller, with different assumptions, found it too. Roder
et al. (2023) recommend exactly this. `consensusISNV()` takes a named list of
objects, one per caller, matches sites by sequence name, position and
alternative allele, and keeps the sites that at least `min_callers` found with a
frequency spread no greater than `freq_tolerance`.

```{r callers-consensus}
gr1 <- GRanges("seg", IRanges::IRanges(c(100, 200, 300), width = 1))
mcols(gr1)$ref <- c("A", "C", "G")
mcols(gr1)$alt <- c("T", "G", "A")
whe1 <- WithinHostExperiment(
    assays = list(altFreq = matrix(c(0.10, 0.20, 0.30), ncol = 1)),
    rowRanges = gr1, colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(sample_id = "S1"))
gr2 <- GRanges("seg", IRanges::IRanges(c(100, 200, 400), width = 1))
mcols(gr2)$ref <- c("A", "C", "T")
mcols(gr2)$alt <- c("T", "G", "C")
whe2 <- WithinHostExperiment(
    assays = list(altFreq = matrix(c(0.12, 0.18, 0.15), ncol = 1)),
    rowRanges = gr2, colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(sample_id = "S1"))
cons_calls <- consensusISNV(list(ivar = whe1, lofreq = whe2))
cons_calls
mcols(SummarizedExperiment::rowRanges(cons_calls))
```
