Two of the four distinct sites survive: positions 100 and 200, found by both
callers with frequency spreads of 0.02, well inside the default tolerance of
0.05. Positions 300 and 400 were each found by one caller only and are gone. The
row metadata records `n_callers`, `caller_names` and `freq_spread` for every
surviving site, so the evidence for each is auditable. Read the `assays(2)` line
in the summary carefully: the consensus object holds `altFreq`, the mean
frequency across callers, and `qcPass` only. Read counts, depths and any
quality-control history are *not* carried over, so run `flagISNV()` on each
caller's own object before taking the consensus, never on the consensus itself.

## Measuring agreement between callers

Before trusting a consensus it is worth knowing how much the callers agreed to
begin with, since a consensus of two callers that disagree about most sites is a
small and possibly biased subset. `calcCallerConcordance()` reports the pairwise
counts and the Jaccard index, the number of shared sites over the number in the
union.

```{r callers-concordance}
calcCallerConcordance(list(ivar = whe1, lofreq = whe2))
```

The pair shares 2 sites, each caller has 1 of its own, and the Jaccard index is
2 over 4, 0.5. A value near 1 means the callers see the same variants and a
consensus costs little; a value near 0 means they disagree about nearly
everything, and then the consensus is not a cleaned-up call set but a third,
smaller one whose properties neither caller's validation covers. With real data
expect Jaccard values well below 1 at low frequencies, which is the whole reason
this check exists. `benchmarkCallers()` extends the comparison with precision,
recall and F1 when a truth set is available.

# Visualisation

## The frequency spectrum of an object

A table of frequencies hides the shape of a distribution, and the shape is what
tells a plausible call set from an implausible one: within-host data should show
many low-frequency variants and few intermediate ones, so a flat or top-heavy
histogram is a reason to look at depth and thresholds. `plotFrequencySpectrum()`
draws that histogram from the passing calls and returns a `ggplot` object, which
can be modified like any other.

```{r viz-spectrum}
#| fig.width: 6
#| fig.height: 4
#| fig.cap: "Allele frequency spectrum."
plotFrequencySpectrum(whe_qc)
```

The horizontal axis is allele frequency and the vertical axis counts sites. With
24 passing calls spread across the whole range, this figure has no shape to
read, which is the point: it is a fixture, and the function is being
demonstrated rather than the data described. Note also that the view is clipped
with coordinate limits rather than by removing data, so a point outside the axis
range is hidden rather than dropped from any summary.

## Donor against recipient

For a transmission pair, the most informative single figure plots each site's
donor frequency against its recipient frequency. Sites on the diagonal were
transmitted and kept their frequency; sites on the axes were present in one host
only; and the spread tells you how much the frequencies were reshuffled, which
is what a bottleneck estimator quantifies.

```{r viz-pair}
#| fig.width: 5
#| fig.height: 5
#| fig.cap: "Donor against recipient frequency."
plotPairScatter(whe_qc, pairId = "pair_1")
```

Each point is one site of the pair. Points along the lower axis are the
donor-only sites counted above, and the five shared sites are those away from
both axes. Because the sites the recipient did not report have no recorded
frequency, their position on this figure is an artefact of how absence is drawn,
not a measurement; the depth split from `calcSharedVariants()` is the honest
version of the same information.

## A quality-control dashboard

When a new data set arrives, the useful first look is several views at once: the
depth distribution, the frequency distribution, the proportion of calls flagged
and the per-sample pass rates. `plotQCDashboard()` assembles them into one
figure, which needs the `r BiocStyle::CRANpkg("patchwork")` package to compose
the panels.

```{r viz-dashboard}
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 6
#| fig.cap: "Four-panel QC dashboard."
plotQCDashboard(whe_qc)
```

The four panels answer the four questions above for this object. What to look
for in your own data is a depth distribution with a long low tail, which tells
you where to set `minDepth`; a frequency distribution piling up at the detection
threshold, which suggests the threshold is doing more than removing noise; and
pass rates that differ markedly between samples, which usually means one library
behaved differently and should be examined before it is pooled with the rest.

## A spectrum object

The site frequency spectrum has its own plotting function, which takes
`WithinHostSFS` objects rather than an experiment, and accepts a named list to
draw several on one pair of axes. That is the comparison the class exists for:
two hosts, two timepoints, or the same sample before and after a correction.

```{r viz-sfs}
#| fig.width: 6
#| fig.height: 4
#| fig.cap: "Folded spectra of the two samples."
plotSFS(list(donor = sfs_donor, recipient = sfs_recip))
```

Each bar is one frequency bin and the colours distinguish the two samples, with
`normalize = TRUE` switching from counts to proportions when the two differ in
size. With 14 and 10 variants in 10 bins, most bars stand at one or zero, which
is the visual form of the warning that `compareSFS()` gave numerically: there is
no shape here to compare. The palette is the colour-blind-safe set of Wong
(2011), recycled beyond eight series.

## A trajectory

Finally, for longitudinal data, `plotFrequencyTrajectory()` draws one line per
variant over time for a named host, which is the figure in which a rising
variant becomes obvious and a transient one reveals itself as a single point.

```{r viz-trajectory}
#| fig.width: 6
#| fig.height: 4
#| fig.cap: "Frequency trajectories, host H1."
plotFrequencyTrajectory(whe_l, hostId = "H1")
```

Two lines are drawn for the two variants of the toy object, over its two
timepoints. With only two timepoints a line cannot show curvature, so this
figure demonstrates the interface rather than any dynamics. In real use, read
such a figure beside the depth at each point: an apparent sweep across a few
percentage points can be the arrival of better coverage rather than of a
variant.

# A worked example on real data

## The data

Every example so far has been synthetic. This section runs the workflow on real
SARS-CoV-2 iSNV calls from Bendall et al. (2023), who sequenced household
transmission pairs in duplicate. The package ships both technical replicates of
two samples from household HH6 as iVar tables, four of the study's 159 calls,
and this section uses the first replicate of each. These are real but very
small, two calls per sample, so they illustrate the workflow rather than
reproduce the study.

One caution about direction. The study's own pair table lists this household in
both directions, as `HH6_A` and `HH6_B`, so it does not establish who infected
whom. We follow `HH6_A` and treat MHM1143 as the donor for illustration only;
nothing below should be read as a claim about the direction of transmission in
this household.

```{r case-import}
donor_file <- system.file("extdata", "MHM1143_rep1.tsv",
    package = "WithinHostExperiment")
recip_file <- system.file("extdata", "MHM1184_rep1.tsv",
    package = "WithinHostExperiment")
whe_sars2 <- readWithinHostTable(
    c(donor_file, recip_file), format = "ivar",
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(
        sample_id = c("MHM1143", "MHM1184"),
        role = c("donor", "recipient"),
        pair_id = c("HH6", "HH6")))
whe_sars2
```

The object holds 4 variant sites across 2 samples, so the two samples' calls do
not overlap at all: two calls each at four distinct positions. One transmission
pair is recognised from the `role` and `pair_id` columns. Four sites is a very
small number, and every quantity below inherits that: the point of the section
is that the code path is the same as for a full study, not that these values
describe the household.

## Recording the genome length

An iVar table carries no reference sequence and no header, so the object arrived
without a recorded genome length, and the per-site indices would refuse to run.
The length belongs to the reference the calls were made against, here the
GenBank record MN908947.3 at 29,903 bases, and it is recorded with the
`seqlengths()` replacement that every Bioconductor ranges object understands.
Recording it on the object, rather than passing it to each function, is what
keeps every per-site quantity dividing by the same number.

```{r case-seqlengths}
GenomeInfoDb::seqlengths(whe_sars2) <- c(MN908947.3 = 29903L)
GenomeInfoDb::seqlengths(whe_sars2)
```

The length is now recorded against the sequence name used in the table. The name
has to match: had the table used `NC_045512.2`, the RefSeq name for the same
genome, assigning to `MN908947.3` would have failed rather than quietly recorded
a length for a sequence with no sites on it. This is the same name-matching
problem the annotation functions guard against.

## Quality control and diversity

With the length recorded, the standard workflow applies: flag the calls that
fail depth and frequency thresholds, summarise the result per sample, then
compute diversity from what passed. The thresholds here, a depth of 100 and a
frequency of 3%, are the Illumina defaults discussed above.

```{r case-qc}
whe_sars2 <- flagISNV(whe_sars2, ISNVFilter(minDepth = 100L, minFreq = 0.03))
qcSummary(whe_sars2)
div_sars2 <- calcDiversity(whe_sars2)
div_sars2
```

The donor kept both of its calls; the recipient kept one of two, at a median
depth of 2,667 reads, so its flagged call failed on frequency rather than depth,
its median frequency of 0.033 sitting just at the threshold. Diversity follows
from what passed: pi of 6.0e-06 for MHM1143 on 2 sites and 2.3e-06 for MHM1184
on 1. Expressed as the units the package's own figures use, those are 0.060 and
0.023 per 10,000 sites. These calls have been through the depth and frequency
filters only, not the replicate-concordance step, so the comparable figure is
the naive median of 0.096 that those figures report across the 83 samples of
this study, not the median of 0.038 after replicate quality control. Both values
sit below that naive median and within a factor of five of it. Two samples
cannot confirm a median, but agreement in order of magnitude is the reassurance
that the units are right, which is the next check.

## Checking the magnitudes

This is where the plausibility check earns its place. The same function that
rejected the synthetic fixture's diversity should accept a real estimate from a
real coronavirus data set, and if it does not, the units or the genome length
are the first suspects.

```{r case-plausibility}
checkDiversityPlausibility(div_sars2, pathogen = "sars_cov_2")
```

Both samples now fall inside the range on both metrics: pi at 6.0e-06 and
2.3e-06 sits within 1e-06 to 1e-03, and the Shannon entropies, 0.38 and 0.16,
are far below the upper bound of 15. Compare this with the synthetic object
earlier, which failed on pi by more than threefold, and the contrast shows what
the check is for. It remains a check on units and orders of magnitude only:
these ranges are the package's own heuristics, and a verdict of `TRUE` is no
evidence that an estimate is correct.

## Transmission

The last step of the workflow asks what the pair shares. With the direction
taken as given and quality control applied, `calcSharedVariants()` counts the
sites in both hosts, in the donor alone and in the recipient alone, splitting
the donor-only count by the recipient's depth as before.

```{r case-transmission}
sv2 <- calcSharedVariants(whe_sars2, pairId = "HH6")
cat("Shared:", sv2$n_shared, "| donor-only:", sv2$n_donor_only,
    "| recipient-only:", sv2$n_recipient_only, "\n")
cat("Donor-only at adequate / low / unknown recipient depth:",
    sv2$n_donor_only_adequate_depth, "/", sv2$n_donor_only_low_depth, "/",
    sv2$n_donor_only_unknown_depth, "\n")
```

No site is shared: 2 donor-only, 1 recipient-only, 3 in all. Both donor-only
sites fall in the unknown-depth group, because an iVar table lists only the
positions with a call, so nothing here records whether the recipient was
sequenced deeply enough at those positions to have detected the variant. That is
the correct conclusion from these two files, and it is a conclusion about data
rather than about transmission. The package's own figures find the same pattern
at scale on this study: of the 52 pairs whose donor carried at least one
concordant iSNV, 47 share none with the recipient. Two limits shape that count.
The study's recipient calls are limited to frequencies of 2 to 98%, so a donor
variant that reached fixation in the recipient also counts as not shared; and in
26 of those pairs the recipient carries no iSNV call at all, so absence of data
is easily recorded as absence of sharing. Bendall et al. (2023) report the
bottleneck estimates for this cohort; these counts describe detection.

# Other pathogens

Nothing in the workflow is specific to SARS-CoV-2. To show that, we run the same
steps on small synthetic fixtures for three further pathogens whose within-host
diversity differs by orders of magnitude, and check each estimate against its
own plausibility range. The files are illustrative fixtures, not measurements,
and the ranges are heuristics, so these sections demonstrate the interface. Each
file is a table without a reference, so the length of the region it covers is
recorded on the object before any per-site index is computed.

## Influenza A

Influenza A has a segmented genome, and here one segment, the 1,701-base
haemagglutinin segment of an H3N2 virus, stands for it. The workflow is
unchanged: record the length, flag with the Illumina preset, compute diversity,
check the magnitudes.

```{r pathogen-flu}
flu_file <- system.file("extdata", "test_influenza_donor.tsv",
    package = "WithinHostExperiment")
whe_flu <- readWithinHostTable(flu_file, format = "ivar",
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(sample_id = "flu_donor"))
GenomeInfoDb::seqlengths(whe_flu) <- c(HA = 1701L)
whe_flu <- flagISNV(whe_flu, adaptiveFilter("illumina"))
div_flu <- calcDiversity(whe_flu, indices = c("pi", "shannon"))
div_flu
checkDiversityPlausibility(div_flu, pathogen = "influenza")
```

The sample has 12 assessed sites and a pi of 2.6e-03 per site with a Shannon
entropy of 6.47, and both fall inside the influenza ranges, 1e-05 to 5e-03 and 0
to 20. Passing here and failing on the SARS-CoV-2 fixture earlier is not a
contradiction: the ranges differ by pathogen because within-host diversity does,
and a short segment carrying a dozen iSNVs is plausible for influenza in a way
it is not for a coronavirus. The estimate is still from a fixture.

## HIV-1

HIV-1 sits at the other end of the scale, with within-host populations an order
of magnitude more diverse than a respiratory virus, and here a 1,000-base window
of the `pol` region stands for one.

```{r pathogen-hiv}
hiv_file <- system.file("extdata", "test_hiv_sample.tsv",
    package = "WithinHostExperiment")
whe_hiv <- readWithinHostTable(hiv_file, format = "ivar",
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(sample_id = "hiv_sample"))
GenomeInfoDb::seqlengths(whe_hiv) <- c(pol = 1000L)
whe_hiv <- flagISNV(whe_hiv, adaptiveFilter("illumina"))
div_hiv <- calcDiversity(whe_hiv, indices = c("pi", "shannon"))
div_hiv
checkDiversityPlausibility(div_hiv, pathogen = "hiv")
```

Twenty assessed sites give a pi of 6.6e-03 and a Shannon entropy of 10.01, both
inside the HIV ranges of 1e-04 to 5e-02 and 0 to 30. Note that this pi is about
two and a half times the influenza value and would have failed the SARS-CoV-2
check comfortably, which is the whole point of choosing the `pathogen` argument
deliberately rather than leaving it at its default.

## Mycobacterium tuberculosis

Tuberculosis is the opposite case: a 4.4-megabase genome with very little
within-host variation, so the per-site diversity is small not because few
variants were found but because they are divided by a large genome.

```{r pathogen-tb}
tb_file <- system.file("extdata", "test_tb_sample.tsv",
    package = "WithinHostExperiment")
whe_tb <- readWithinHostTable(tb_file, format = "ivar",
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(sample_id = "tb_sample"))
GenomeInfoDb::seqlengths(whe_tb) <- c(Rv0001 = 4411532L)
whe_tb <- flagISNV(whe_tb, adaptiveFilter("illumina"))
div_tb <- calcDiversity(whe_tb, indices = c("pi", "shannon"))
div_tb
checkDiversityPlausibility(div_tb, pathogen = "tb")
```

Three sites give a pi of 6.4e-08 and a Shannon entropy of 0.58, inside the
tuberculosis ranges of 1e-09 to 1e-04 and 0 to 5. The five orders of magnitude
between this pi and the HIV one above come mostly from the denominator, which is
why a per-site index quoted without its genome length is uninterpretable, and
why this package records the length on the object and reads it from there.

## Neutrality statistics across the three

Running the same statistic on all three makes the dependence on the number of
sites visible, which is the lesson worth taking from this section. The genome
length is read back off each object rather than retyped, and the table reports
`n_sites` beside each statistic so that nothing can be read without it.

```{r pathogen-neutrality}
nt_flu <- calcNeutralityTests(whe_flu,
    genomeLength = sum(GenomeInfoDb::seqlengths(whe_flu)))
nt_hiv <- calcNeutralityTests(whe_hiv,
    genomeLength = sum(GenomeInfoDb::seqlengths(whe_hiv)))
nt_tb  <- calcNeutralityTests(whe_tb,
    genomeLength = sum(GenomeInfoDb::seqlengths(whe_tb)))
data.frame(
    pathogen = c("Influenza", "HIV-1", "M. tuberculosis"),
    n_sites = c(nt_flu$n_sites, nt_hiv$n_sites, nt_tb$n_sites),
    tajimaD = c(nt_flu$tajimaD, nt_hiv$tajimaD, nt_tb$tajimaD),
    fusFs = c(nt_flu$fusFs, nt_hiv$fusFs, nt_tb$fusFs))
```

The influenza and HIV fixtures give positive Tajima's D, 2.37 on 12 sites and
2.12 on 20, and the tuberculosis fixture gives -0.91 on 3. Read the `n_sites`
column first: 3 is the smallest number at which D is defined at all, since below
three segregating sites it is a function of one or two frequencies rather than
of a spectrum and `tajimaD()` returns `NA` with a warning. A D computed from
exactly three sites is formally defined and practically meaningless, and these
are synthetic files besides, so no sign in this table carries any biological
meaning. In real within-host data a negative D or Fs is often read as purifying
selection or as expansion after a bottleneck, and a positive one as balancing
selection or population structure; either reading needs far more sites than
these fixtures hold, and the deep-sequencing caveats above apply to all of them.

# Scope and limitations

This package operates at the level of individual single nucleotide variants. It
does not perform the following, and we list them so that the boundary is
explicit rather than discovered.

**Haplotype phasing and quasispecies reconstruction.** Knowing which variants
travel together on the same genome requires read-level analysis of alignments,
which is outside what a `RangedSummarizedExperiment` of per-site calls can
express. For haplotype-aware analysis consider CliqueSNV (Knyazev et al. 2021,
*Nucleic Acids Res* 49:e102) or ShoRAH (Zagordi et al. 2011, *BMC
Bioinformatics* 12:119). Their output can be imported here for downstream
diversity and quality-control work.

**Telling co-infection from within-host diversity.** Two distinct infecting
lineages and one diversifying lineage can produce similar per-site frequency
patterns, and separating them needs phylogenetic analysis of full haplotypes.
The multi-caller consensus and replicate-concordance steps reduce artefacts but
do not address this at all.

**Drift-aware selection inference.** `estimateSelectionCoefficient()` fits a
deterministic logit-frequency model, which attributes all frequency change to
selection. For inference that separates selection from drift, use a dedicated
Wright-Fisher or diffusion-based framework.

**Neutrality testing as a formal test.** Tajima's D and Fu's Fs are reported
here as descriptions of the frequency spectrum. Because sequencing reads are not
independent lineages, their null distributions do not apply to deep-sequencing
data, and a p-value computed from them would not mean what it appears to.
Simulation that models the read-sampling process is the rigorous route.

**Validating the estimators.** Nothing in this vignette validates any estimator.
The fixtures are synthetic, the real example is two samples, and the
plausibility ranges are heuristics of the package's own. Where a number is
wanted for comparison, the package's figure script computes it from the public
data and records it.

# Glossary

**Allele frequency.** The proportion of reads at a site carrying the
non-reference base.

**Bottleneck.** The number of viral genomes founding the infection in a
recipient, written Nb; a small bottleneck loses most of the donor's variation by
chance.

**Consensus sequence.** The reference with each of a sample's substitutions at
or above a frequency, usually 0.5, written in; it represents the single
commonest genome in a host.

**Detection threshold.** The lowest allele frequency a call may have and be
kept, below which variants are treated as unobservable.

**dN/dS.** The ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitutions per site
between two sequences, usually with a multiple-hit correction; a divergence
measure, unlike pN/pS.

**Folded and unfolded spectrum.** A folded site frequency spectrum bins the
minor allele frequency from the threshold to 0.5 and claims nothing about
ancestry; an unfolded one bins the alternative allele frequency from the
threshold to 1 and treats the reference allele as ancestral.

**iSNV.** Intra-host single nucleotide variant: a single-base difference
segregating within one host's pathogen population.

**Nucleotide diversity (pi).** The expected number of differences per site
between two genomes drawn at random from the host.

**pN/pS.** The ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous polymorphism per site within
one host; expected near 1 with no selection, below 1 under purifying selection.

**Primer site.** A region where amplification primers bind, in which an apparent
variant may be an artefact of the protocol and is therefore masked.

**QC flag.** An entry of the logical `qcPass` matrix set to `FALSE` by a
quality-control step; the call is retained and marked, never deleted.

**Read depth.** The number of reads covering a site in a sample.

**Shannon entropy.** A measure of how uncertain the allele carried by a randomly
chosen read is, summed over sites, so it rises with both the number and the
evenness of variants.

**Site frequency spectrum.** The distribution of allele frequencies across a
sample's variant sites, from which the neutrality statistics are computed.

**Strand bias.** A variant supported overwhelmingly by reads from one strand,
which suggests systematic error rather than a real variant present on both
strands.

**Synonymous and nonsynonymous.** A substitution in a coding sequence that
leaves the amino acid unchanged is synonymous; one that alters it is
nonsynonymous, and one that creates a stop codon is nonsense.

**Tajima's D.** The normalised difference between nucleotide diversity and
Watterson's theta; negative under an excess of rare variants, positive under an
excess of intermediate-frequency ones.

**Technical replicate.** A second sequencing of the same biological sample, used
to distinguish genuine low-frequency variants from artefacts.

**Transmission pair.** Two samples from different hosts, one believed to have
infected the other, declared with the `role` and `pair_id` columns of
`colData()`.

# Session information

A vignette that cannot be traced to the versions that produced it cannot be
reproduced, and Bioconductor packages change between releases. The chunk below
records the R version, the platform and the exact version of every attached and
loaded package, which is the first thing to compare when an output here differs
from the one on your own machine.

```{r session}
sessionInfo()
```

The output lists the R version and platform, then the attached packages, then
those loaded only through a namespace. Note that the `pkgload` or
development-version entries that sometimes appear mean the package was not
installed from a Bioconductor release, in which case differences from the
published vignette are expected.
